triage.name: Birthmarks
triage.reason: Visible skin lesion with a differential (hemangioma, nevus, Mongolian spot) reachable by history and exam; good MSK & skin case.

review_issues: presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: Present at birth or appear in the first weeks of life in most cases
Certain pigmented birthmarks are more common in infants with darker skin (Mongolian spots, café-au-lait macules)
Congenital melanocytic nevi are present in about 1% of newborns
Infantile hemangiomas are more common in premature and low-birth-weight infants

risk_factors.text: Premature birth or low birth weight (infantile hemangioma)
Family history of a similar birthmark

family_history: Similar birthmark in a parent or sibling

chief_complaints.text: My baby has a mark on the skin that was there when she was born
There is a red spot that seems to be getting bigger
There is a brown or blue patch on the skin

hpi.onset: Present at birth, or noticed by the parents in the first days to weeks of life
hpi.duration: Since birth; some lesions appear or enlarge over the first months
hpi.progression: Pigmented birthmarks are usually stable or grow with the child; infantile hemangiomas may grow for several months and then slowly fade; port-wine stains stay the same or darken with age
hpi.location: Anywhere on the skin; commonly the face, scalp, trunk, buttocks or lower back
hpi.quality: A flat or raised colored patch or bump; may be red, pink, tan, brown, gray, blue or black
hpi.severity: Usually painless and not bothersome; some hemangiomas can ulcerate or bleed
aggravating: Rubbing or trauma can make a vascular birthmark bleed
relieving: Nothing specific; most need no treatment

associated_symptoms.text: The mark grows or changes color over weeks to months
The mark is raised and warm
The mark itches or is tender

pertinent_negatives: A new mole that changes shape, color or size after childhood

positives.text: A colored patch or bump on the skin
The mark changes size or color over time

argues_against: A rapidly growing, irregular, multicolored lesion with bleeding (melanoma)
A birthmark associated with a syndrome involving the nervous system

atypical.how_it_differs: Infantile hemangiomas may not be visible at birth and appear in the first weeks, then grow rapidly before fading; some are deep and look bluish rather than red.
A birthmark that has been present for years may be noticed only when it changes; any new change in a long-standing mole needs evaluation for melanoma.

general.mild: Well-appearing infant, alert, feeding normally, no distress
general.moderate: Well-appearing but the lesion is raised, warm or crusted; infant may be fussy when it is touched
general.severe: Ill-appearing with an ulcerated or bleeding lesion; may be uncomfortable or feeding poorly
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, lethargic, with an actively bleeding or infected lesion

findings.maneuver: Inspect the entire skin surface in good light, undressing the infant, and note the size, color, shape, border and surface of the mark
findings.finding: A circumscribed colored patch or raised lesion present since birth or the first weeks of life

findings.maneuver: Inspect and gently palpate the lesion
findings.finding: A red or pink vascular lesion; a port-wine stain is flat and blanchable, an infantile hemangioma is raised, warm and may be lobulated

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lesion with a bright light and compare with surrounding skin
findings.finding: A flat tan, brown, gray, blue or black macule or patch (café-au-lait macule, Mongolian spot, congenital melanocytic nevus)

findings.maneuver: Press the lesion with a finger or glass slide
findings.finding: The lesion blanches with pressure, favoring a vascular birthmark over a pigmented one

findings.maneuver: Press a clear glass slide or finger over the lesion
findings.finding: The color does not blanch, favoring a pigmented birthmark such as a nevus or Mongolian spot

findings.maneuver: Measure the longest diameter and record the location and number of lesions
findings.finding: A single or few lesions with stable size; multiple or large lesions may suggest a syndrome

findings.maneuver: Inspect the surface of the lesion for breakdown
findings.finding: Ulceration, crusting or bleeding, most often in a rapidly growing infantile hemangioma

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate for warmth, spreading erythema or purulent drainage
findings.finding: Warmth, spreading redness, purulent discharge or foul odor suggesting secondary infection

findings.maneuver: Gently palpate the lesion and surrounding skin
findings.finding: No tenderness, no induration and no fluctuance

findings.maneuver: Palpate the cervical, axillary and inguinal lymph node basins
findings.finding: No enlarged or tender lymph nodes

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for liver and spleen size
Assess tone, spontaneous movement, reflexes and alertness
findings.finding: Normal tone, movement and neurologic exam for age

findings.maneuver: Review weight, length and head circumference on the growth chart and ask about feeding
findings.finding: Normal growth parameters and feeding for age

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa, lips and conjunctivae

imaging.study: MRI brain and orbits with and without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Large facial segmental hemangioma in a beard, periorbital or frontonasal distribution, or any concern for PHACE syndrome

findings.text: Intracranial vascular anomaly (arterial anomalies, coarctation, aberrant carotid) suggesting PHACE syndrome

imaging.study: MRI spine with and without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Large or multiple lumbosacral lesions, or a lesion with a dimple, hair tuft or other marker of occult spinal dysraphism

findings.text: Tethered cord or intraspinal extension of the lesion

imaging.preferred_when: Soft tissue or deep vascular lesion when the diagnosis is uncertain

findings.text: Well-defined soft tissue mass with internal vascular flow
High-flow vascular channels consistent with hemangioma

imaging.preferred_when: Six or more café-au-lait macules, or other features suggesting neurofibromatosis type 1
A lesion that is changing, bleeding or has features concerning for melanoma or another malignancy

initial.why: Inspect the entire skin surface in good light, measure and document the lesion, and look for features that suggest a syndrome

confirmatory.why: Confirms the diagnosis when a lesion is changing, bleeding or has features concerning for melanoma or another malignancy
confirmatory.only_if: the lesion is changing, bleeding, or has features concerning for melanoma or another malignancy

supporting.test: MRI brain and orbits with and without contrast
supporting.only_if: large facial segmental hemangioma in a beard, periorbital or frontonasal distribution, or concern for PHACE syndrome

supporting.test: MRI spine with and without contrast
supporting.only_if: large or multiple lumbosacral lesions, or a lesion with a dimple, hair tuft or other marker of occult spinal dysraphism

supporting.why: Characterizes a soft tissue or deep vascular lesion when the diagnosis is uncertain
Screens for intra-abdominal lesions in suspected neurofibromatosis type 1
supporting.only_if: six or more café-au-lait macules or other features suggesting neurofibromatosis type 1

not_indicated.why: Not needed for an uncomplicated birthmark
Not needed for an uncomplicated birthmark
Not needed unless there is concern for secondary infection
Not needed unless there is concern for secondary infection
Not needed for an uncomplicated birthmark
Not needed unless a malignancy is suspected
Not needed for an uncomplicated birthmark
Not useful for evaluating a skin birthmark
Exposes the child to radiation and is rarely needed for a birthmark

decision_points: Any changing, bleeding or irregular lesion in an older child or adult should be evaluated for melanoma
Large facial segmental hemangiomas warrant evaluation for PHACE syndrome
Lumbosacral lesions with a dimple, hair tuft or other marker warrant imaging for occult spinal dysraphism
Six or more café-au-lait macules should prompt evaluation for neurofibromatosis type 1

differential.name: Melanoma
differential.why_considered: A pigmented lesion that is changing, bleeding or irregular can be a melanoma rather than a benign birthmark
differential.trigger: Any pigmented lesion that changes in size, shape or color, bleeds, itches or becomes tender

history: New or changing lesion rather than one stable since birth
Bleeding, itching or pain in the lesion
Family history of melanoma
History of sunburn or intense sun exposure
exam: Asymmetry, irregular border, multiple colors, diameter over 6 mm
Elevation or surface change in a previously flat lesion
Satellite lesions or surrounding erythema
labs: No routine lab confirms melanoma; LDH may be elevated with advanced disease
imaging: Dermoscopy showing atypical pigment network, irregular streaks or blue-white veil

differential.name: Kaposi sarcoma
differential.why_considered: Violaceous or red-purple vascular-appearing lesions can mimic a vascular birthmark
differential.trigger: Multiple violaceous lesions in an immunocompromised patient or an older adult, especially with lymphadenopathy

history: HIV infection, transplant immunosuppression or older age
Lesions appearing in adulthood rather than at birth
Weight loss, fever or night sweats
exam: Violaceous macules, plaques or nodules on skin or mucosa
Lymphadenopathy
Oral or conjunctival lesions
imaging: Biopsy showing spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces and HHV-8 positivity

differential.name: Congenital melanocytic nevus
differential.why_considered: A pigmented birthmark present at birth that can be mistaken for other pigmented lesions

history: Present at birth and grows proportionally with the child
Usually stable color and shape over time
exam: Well-circumscribed brown to black macule, papule or plaque
May have hair growth or a cobblestone surface
No ulceration or bleeding
imaging: Biopsy only if atypical features develop

differential.name: Café-au-lait macule
differential.why_considered: A flat tan-brown birthmark that can be confused with other pigmented lesions

history: Present at birth or early infancy
Stable, uniform color
Family history of neurofibromatosis type 1 if multiple
exam: Uniform light brown macule with smooth borders
Six or more lesions over 5 mm in prepubertal children suggests neurofibromatosis type 1
Look for axillary freckling, neurofibromas or Lisch nodules
imaging: MRI brain or spine only if features of neurofibromatosis type 1 are present

differential.name: Mongolian spot (dermal melanocytosis)
differential.why_considered: A blue-gray pigmented birthmark often mistaken for a bruise or other lesion

history: Present at birth
More common in infants with darker skin
Does not change or fade quickly
exam: Blue-gray macule or patch on the buttocks or lower back
Does not blanch
No tenderness or swelling
imaging: Not indicated unless lumbosacral lesion has a dimple, hair tuft or other marker of occult spinal dysraphism

differential.name: Port-wine stain (capillary malformation)
differential.why_considered: A red vascular birthmark that can be confused with an infantile hemangioma

history: Present at birth
Grows proportionally with the child
Does not involute
exam: Flat, pink to red patch that blanches with pressure
Sharp midline demarcation possible
May darken and thicken with age
imaging: MRI brain if Sturge-Weber syndrome is suspected (facial port-wine stain in V1 distribution with seizures or developmental delay)

differential.name: Infantile hemangioma
differential.why_considered: A red raised vascular birthmark that can be confused with other vascular lesions

history: May not be visible at birth; appears in first weeks
Rapid growth over months then slow involution
More common in premature or low-birth-weight infants
exam: Raised, warm, lobulated red lesion
Blanches with pressure
May ulcerate or bleed during rapid growth
imaging: Ultrasound showing high-flow vascular channels if diagnosis uncertain
MRI brain and orbits if large facial segmental hemangioma suggests PHACE syndrome

severity.mild: A small, stable, uncomplicated birthmark that is not changing and does not bother the patient
severity.moderate: A birthmark that is growing, raised, or has surface changes such as crusting or mild ulceration, but without bleeding or infection
severity.severe: An ulcerated or bleeding birthmark, or one associated with a syndrome requiring further evaluation
severity.critical: A birthmark with active hemorrhage, secondary infection with systemic signs, or airway compromise from a large facial or neck lesion

red_flags.finding: A pigmented lesion that changes in size, shape or color, or becomes symptomatic
red_flags.meaning: Possible melanoma; needs urgent dermatologic evaluation and biopsy

red_flags.finding: Bleeding, itching or pain in a long-standing mole
Large facial segmental hemangioma in a beard, periorbital or frontonasal distribution
red_flags.meaning: Evaluate for PHACE syndrome and possible airway or visual compromise

red_flags.finding: Lumbosacral lesion with a dimple, hair tuft or other marker
red_flags.meaning: Possible occult spinal dysraphism; needs MRI spine

red_flags.finding: Ulceration with spreading erythema, warmth or purulent drainage

complications.name: Ulceration and bleeding
clues: Crusting or breakdown of the surface

complications.name: Malignant transformation of a congenital melanocytic nevus
clues: Change in size, color or shape

special_populations.differences: Most birthmarks are benign and require only observation; infantile hemangiomas may grow rapidly in the first months and then involute; large lesions may need treatment to prevent complications.
Premature and low-birth-weight infants have a higher risk of infantile hemangiomas; lesions may not be visible at birth and appear in the first weeks.
A long-standing birthmark that changes should raise concern for melanoma; new lesions in adulthood are less likely to be birthmarks.
Hormonal changes can cause darkening or enlargement of pigmented lesions; any changing lesion should be evaluated for melanoma.

key_questions.question: When did you first notice the mark — was it there at birth, or did it appear later?
key_questions.looking_for: Present at birth or in the first weeks of life; a lesion appearing later in childhood or adulthood is less likely a birthmark

key_questions.question: Has the mark changed in size, shape, or color since you first noticed it?
key_questions.looking_for: Stable or growing proportionally with the child; rapid change, darkening, or new irregularity raises concern for melanoma

key_questions.question: Does the mark bleed, itch, hurt, or crust over?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in a simple birthmark; bleeding, itching, or pain in a pigmented lesion suggests malignant transformation

key_questions.question: Is the mark raised, warm, or growing quickly?
key_questions.looking_for: A raised, warm, rapidly enlarging red lesion suggests an infantile hemangioma in its growth phase

key_questions.question: Where is the mark located, and is it flat or raised?
key_questions.looking_for: Facial, lumbosacral, or segmental distribution; lumbosacral lesions with a dimple or hair tuft raise concern for occult spinal dysraphism

key_questions.question: How many similar marks does the child have?
key_questions.looking_for: Six or more café-au-lait macules suggests neurofibromatosis type 1

key_questions.question: Has the child had any seizures, developmental delay, or vision problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizures or developmental delay with a facial port-wine stain suggests Sturge-Weber syndrome

key_questions.question: Does anyone else in the family have a similar birthmark or a history of skin cancer?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of neurofibromatosis type 1, melanoma, or similar lesions

key_questions.question: Was the baby born prematurely or with a low birth weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Prematurity and low birth weight increase the risk of infantile hemangioma

key_questions.question: Is the child feeding well, gaining weight, and acting normally?
key_questions.looking_for: Normal feeding and growth; poor feeding or lethargy suggests systemic illness or a syndrome

key_questions.question: Has the mark ever been infected, ulcerated, or needed treatment?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior ulceration, bleeding, or infection, especially in a hemangioma

key_questions.question: Is there any history of immunosuppression, HIV, or transplant in the patient?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression raises concern for Kaposi sarcoma in violaceous lesions

reasoning_points: The lesion was present at birth or appeared in the first weeks of life, consistent with a congenital malformation rather than an acquired lesion
The mark is stable or grows proportionally with the child, without rapid change, bleeding, or itching
The lesion is well-circumscribed and has a characteristic color and surface for its type (red vascular vs. tan, brown, blue, or black pigmented)
Blanching with pressure favors a vascular birthmark; failure to blanch favors a pigmented lesion
No systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, poor feeding, or lethargy
No features suggesting a syndrome: no large facial segmental hemangioma, no lumbosacral dimple or hair tuft, fewer than six café-au-lait macules
No features concerning for malignancy: no irregular borders, multiple colors, recent growth, or bleeding in a pigmented lesion
The clinical appearance is sufficient for diagnosis in most cases; biopsy is reserved for lesions with atypical or concerning features

easy: Newborn with a classic flat salmon patch or Mongolian spot noted on routine exam
Infant with a typical strawberry hemangioma that appeared in the first weeks and is growing
Well-appearing child with a single stable brown macule present since birth
No red flags on history or exam
medium: Infant with a raised red lesion that is enlarging and beginning to crust
Child with several café-au-lait macules requiring evaluation for neurofibromatosis type 1
Lumbosacral lesion with a small dimple requiring imaging for occult spinal dysraphism
Lesion whose color is difficult to classify as vascular versus pigmented
hard: Older child or adult with a long-standing pigmented lesion that is now changing, raising concern for melanoma
Immunocompromised patient with multiple violaceous lesions mimicking a vascular birthmark (Kaposi sarcoma)
Large facial segmental hemangioma with concern for PHACE syndrome or airway compromise
Facial port-wine stain with seizures or developmental delay suggesting Sturge-Weber syndrome
Lesion with secondary infection or active bleeding requiring urgent management
